title: Saltimbocca alla Romana
subtitle: Pork escalopes with sage and pancetta in butter
excerpt: Saltimbocca translates as 'jumps in the mouth', and this Roman dish earns the name. Thin pork escalopes are topped with sage and wrapped in pancetta, then pan-fried in butter until golden. The whole thing takes about 15 minutes.
sourceNotes: Saltimbocca is a Roman classic, though similar dishes appear across central Italy. The traditional version uses veal, but pork escalopes work just as well and are more widely available.

content.text: Bash the pork escalopes between two sheets of cling film to an even 5mm thickness before you do anything else. Even thickness means even cooking. Thin slices of pancetta crisping around the edges is the goal.

items.prepNote: cut into 4 escalopes and bashed thin

content.text: Lay 2 sage leaves on top of each pork escalope. Lay a slice of pancetta over the sage and press firmly so it sticks. Secure with a toothpick if needed.
Season the pork side lightly with pepper only (the pancetta brings the salt). Dust the pork side lightly in flour and shake off the excess.

Heat the butter and olive oil in a large frying pan over a medium-high heat. When the butter is foaming, place the escalopes pancetta-side down. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the pancetta is crisp and golden.
Flip and cook on the pork side for 2 to 3 minutes until cooked through. Transfer to a warm plate to rest briefly.
Serve with lemon wedges and the pan juices spooned over.

items.cause: Pan was not hot enough when the meat went in.
items.fix: Raise the heat and press the pancetta flat against the pan.

items.symptom: Butter burned before the pork was done
items.cause: Heat too high for butter alone.
items.fix: Add more olive oil to cool it down and carry on.
Use a toothpick to pin the layers together next time.
